chapter_theme: A song at Thirumayendram (திருமயேந்திரம்): the poet describes women who rejoice at gold and, when it is gone, hand a man the begging bowl and staff and poison him, and asks whether he must wander as a dog; the praise names the vel that ground the asuras while Death swung his noose.

763.reading: The poet describes women with bee-haunted hair, arrow eyes, pearl teeth, cuckoo voices and creeper waists who rejoice and chatter when they see gold, gossip, flatter and dance making eyes whirl, cheats who, when the gold is gone, hand a man the begging bowl and staff and say 'go', and even give poison, and asks whether he, a dog, must wander and perish for them. The praise tells how, when the gods and sages and Brahma cried out, Murugan came saying 'fear not' and threw the vel that crushed the asuras, turned mountains to dust while Death swung his noose, names him son of Siva with the ash and serpent and moon in his hair, and lover of the moon-faced girl who has entered the poet's heart, at Mayendram.
763.nuance: பொன் கண்டவுடன் களிகூர்ந்து and கஞ்சுளியும் தடியும் ஈந்து போ என: the women's welcome begins at gold and ends by sending the man away as a beggar. அந்தகனும் கயிறு ஆங்கை வீசிட turns Death's noose against the asuras. என்றன் உளம் புகு பாங்கி மானொடு is uncertain: the doe may be Valli, and பாங்கி may be her companion.

links.note: The Naladiyar says courtesans would bow to Mal himself yet send away a man with nothing in his hand; 763 shows them handing the ruined man a begging bowl and staff.

763 says the women, once the gold is gone, hand a man the begging bowl and staff, say 'go', and even give poison (கஞ்சுளியும் தடியும் ஈந்து போ என நஞ்சை இடும்). Naladiyar 374 says that to such women a man without money is poison and a rich oil-presser sugar (காணம் இலாதார் கடுவனையர் ... அக்காரம் அன்னார்). Poison belongs to the same reckoning in both: the moneyless man is poison to them in the quatrain, and in the song they give him poison.
